newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - French govt to discuss budget on Thursday.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - French govt to discuss budget on Thursday.

text.p: The French government will discuss measures on Thursday to curb the budget deficit, but Prime Minister Lionel Jospin will make a final decision, government spokeswoman Catherine Trautmann said on Wednesday.

The Socialist-led government is due to announce the measures shortly after it releases results on Monday of a public finances audit, expected to show the deficit running at 3.5 percent or more of gross domestic product (GDP).
Jospin has called a special meeting of his ministers for 0930 GMT on Thursday.

"We have a working meeting tomorrow which will examine the measures which could accompany the estimates (in the audit)," Trautmann told a news conference after the cabinet meeting. "The prime minister will then, make a decision on the different measures he wants to take."
She said she could not comment on the size of the budget deficit since the government had not received the audit being carried out by two members of the Court of Auditors.
She noted that former prime minister Alain Juppe had made his own statement on the size of the deficit.

Figures in a letter from Juppe to Jospin leaked last week suggested the deficit would be around 3.5 percent of GDP without action, compared to 3.0 percent forecast in the 1997 Finance Act passed by the previous centre-right government.
President Jacques Chirac said on Monday the deficit was around 3.5 percent of GDP.
"We do not have the figures. I cannot comment on them," Trautmann said, when asked about Chirac's statement.
But she said figures being quoted "are not automatically those which we will be working on tomorrow."

The government has pledged to act to reduce the deficit but has said it will not impose new austerity measures just to cut it to precisely 3.0 percent of GDP, the goal stated in the Maastricht Treaty for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
The Maastricht Treaty says government budget deficits must be cut to or moving towards three percent this year for a country to qualify for EMU.
Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn has suggested measures to reduce the deficit could include a mix of savings and tax increases on companies and well-off households.
Afternoon daily Le Monde said on Wednesday the government could increase company taxes for one year only, though Trautmann's comments suggested no decision has been made.
Strauss-Kahn has said no measures will hit investment, which is badly needed to revive economic growth.
Strauss-Kahn also told reporters on Wednesday he hoped the deficit would be as low as possible.

"I hope that this deficit will turn out to be as low as possible. Obviously, unfortunately, it will be above three percent since it is clear the previous government let things overrun," he said. "We will see what the auditors tell us...when the report is handed to the government at the end of the week."
